title: Absolute optimality gap
definition: The difference B − L between valid upper and lower bounds on the optimal objective value. A positive gap leaves uncertainty; it does not alone prove a current feasible answer is suboptimal.
example: Bounds L = 6 and B = 10 leave an absolute gap of 4. Relative-gap conventions depend on the solver.

title: Best-known feasible solution
definition: The best feasible candidate found in a stated search or comparison record. It may be globally optimal already, but the record alone need not prove that.
example: Recording only 0, 2 and 4 makes x = 2 best recorded in OPT-004, while the global answer is 8.

title: Binary variable
definition: An integer variable whose only permitted values are 0 and 1, often representing an off/on or no/yes choice.
example: A yes/no operating choice can use 1 for operate and 0 for stay idle.

title: Constraint
definition: A condition that every feasible solution must satisfy. A candidate must pass all model constraints as well as its decision domain.
example: Point (4, 4) fits x + y ≤ 8 but violates 2x + y ≤ 10.

title: Continuous variable
definition: A variable allowed to take any real value in its domain, subject to the constraints. A slider with discrete steps can only sample that continuous domain.
example: LAB-B allows fractional activity-hours, even though its sliders move in half-hour steps.

title: Decision domain
definition: The permitted type and range of a decision variable before any additional restrictions are imposed. The domain is part of the model.
example: A fleet may require integer n from 0 to 12; activity-hours x may be continuous from 0 to 10.

title: Decision variable
definition: A quantity the model allows you to choose. Its permitted values are set by its domain and the model constraints.
example: Fleet size n is chosen; the available fleet A is supplied as an input.

title: Exhaustive enumeration
definition: Checking every candidate in a finite decision domain, then comparing the feasible objective values. Complete, correct evaluation can prove the global optimum within that finite model.
example: OPT-001 checks all 13 fleet sizes from 0 through 12 and identifies n = 8 with profit $220.

title: Feasible set
definition: The collection of all candidates satisfying the domain and every constraint. It is the intersection of their allowed sets and includes permitted boundaries.
example: LAB-B can produce a polygon, an included line segment, a single point or an empty set.

title: Feasible solution
definition: A candidate satisfying the variable domain and every model constraint. Feasibility alone says nothing about whether its objective value is best.
example: Under LAB-B defaults, (3, 4) satisfies time, staffing and the 0–10 domain.

title: Global optimum
definition: A feasible decision at least as good as every feasible alternative for the stated objective. It is also locally optimal, but a local optimum need not be global.
example: At U = 10, x = 8 is globally optimal because no feasible score exceeds 10 and f(8) = 10.

title: Heuristic
definition: A method intended to find useful solutions without a general guarantee of proving the global optimum. Its candidates still need independent feasibility checks.
example: Stopping at the first local peak can find x = 2 in OPT-004 while missing the taller peak at 8.

title: Infeasible candidate
definition: A candidate that violates at least one constraint or its domain. One failed candidate does not establish that the whole model is infeasible.
example: At U = 5, x = 8 has score 10 but is excluded from OPT-004’s feasible choices.

title: Infeasible model
definition: A model with no candidate satisfying all its rules. This means its feasible set is empty, not merely that a search record contains no feasible candidate.
example: Requiring x + y ≥ 9 and x + y ≤ 8 simultaneously makes LAB-B infeasible.

title: Integer variable
definition: A variable restricted to whole-number values in its domain. A fractional value is not feasible merely because it satisfies resource inequalities.
example: OPT-001 permits 0, 1, …, 12 vehicles; 4.5 vehicles is outside that domain.

title: Local optimum
definition: A feasible decision at least as good as every sufficiently nearby feasible alternative. For maximization it is a local maximum; it need not be globally best.
example: With U = 10, x = 2 is a genuine local peak of score 6, but x = 8 has score 10.

title: Lower bound
definition: A justified value no larger than the true optimal objective value. For maximization a feasible score gives a lower bound; for minimization a lower bound limits how small the optimum can be.
example: The feasible score f(2) = 6 supplies a lower bound of 6 on OPT-004’s default maximum.

title: Maximization
definition: An objective direction that prefers larger values among feasible choices. Global maximization compares against every feasible alternative.
example: OPT-002 can maximize profit or revenue; those different goals can select different fleets.

title: Minimization
definition: An objective direction that prefers smaller values among feasible choices. Constraints still determine which choices may compete.
example: With no minimum-service rule, cost minimization in OPT-002 can select zero vehicles.

title: Objective function
definition: The rule that computes the quantity to maximize or minimize from a candidate decision. It ranks feasible choices; it does not replace their constraints.
example: P(n) = 80n − 5n² − 100 computes the synthetic fleet profit.

title: Objective value
definition: The numerical result of evaluating the objective at a particular candidate. An infeasible candidate can have an arithmetic value without being an allowed solution.
example: In OPT-004, f(2) = 6 is a candidate value; the default global optimal value is 10.

title: Optimal value
definition: The supremum of feasible objective values for maximization, or infimum for minimization. An optimizer attains it; some models can approach their optimal value without attaining it.
example: OPT-004 at U = 6 has optimal value 6 and two optimizers. Maximizing x on 0 < x < 1 approaches 1 without attaining it.

title: Optimality certificate
definition: Evidence establishing that a feasible decision attains the global optimum. Matching valid bounds or exact enumeration of a finite domain can provide such evidence.
example: The bound f(x) ≤ 10 together with feasible f(8) = 10 certifies the default global answer in OPT-004.

title: Optimization
definition: Choosing the best feasible decision for a stated objective and model. The claim of best needs evidence covering the permitted choices.
example: In OPT-001, evaluating all 13 fleet sizes proves that 8 vehicles maximize the synthetic profit.

title: Optimizer
definition: A feasible decision attaining the model’s optimal objective value. Several different decisions can be optimizers; the decision is distinct from its numerical score.
example: At U = 6, both x = 2 and x = 6 optimize OPT-004. The shared value is 6.

title: Parameter
definition: An input treated as fixed while a particular model is solved. Changing it creates a different model instance or scenario.
example: Budget B = 260 is a parameter; selected fleet size n is a decision.

title: Slack
definition: For an upper-limit inequality, the right side minus the left side at a feasible point. Zero slack means equality. For a lower limit, the analogous excess above its minimum is called surplus.
example: At (3, 4), the time rule x + y ≤ 8 has slack 8 − 7 = 1 hour.

title: Tight constraint
definition: A constraint holding with equality at the point considered. Tightness alone does not prove that relaxing it improves an objective. It differs from simply switching a rule on.
example: At (3, 4), staffing 2x + y ≤ 10 is tight, while time x + y ≤ 8 is not.

title: Trade-off
definition: Gaining one quantity while giving up another under shared limitations. A resource substitution does not by itself determine which feasible plan is preferable.
example: Moving from (3, 4) to (4, 2) gains one A-hour and gives up two B-hours while using the same staffing.

title: Upper bound
definition: A justified value no smaller than the true optimal objective value. For maximization it limits possible improvement; for minimization a feasible objective value supplies an upper bound.
example: In default OPT-004, f(x) ≤ 10 for every feasible x supplies an upper bound of 10 on the maximum.
